transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date/Time: 2025-11-29 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Lead ML Eng, Northfield), Asha Patel (Platform Eng), Simon Green (CTO)

Auto-generated Summary (brief):
Quickstart SDK walkthrough focused on Python + TypeScript examples, auth patterns (API keys, SSO/SAML, KMS for secrets), sandbox env setup, and a short discussion on hosted vs dedicated vs private for latency/cost. Agreed next steps: share quickstart repo, run a small benchmark, and sync on security checklist.

Topics: SDK quickstart, auth & secrets, sandbox provisioning, CI/CD secrets rotation, VPC/private deployment tradeoffs, Optimize (batching/caching) suggestions.

Transcript Body:
[00:00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, I'm the AE working with you on the Northfield project. With me is Priya, our SE, who will run most of the dev walkthrough. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:08] Carlos Mendes: Good, thanks. Excited to get into the SDK part. We've looked at the docs but want to see real env setup and auth.
[00:00:15] Asha Patel: Hi, yeah we're mostly responsible for infra and CI. We want to make sure keys, rotation, and VPC options are clear.
[00:00:19] Priya Nambiar: Great, that's exactly what we'll cover. Quick agenda: 1) repo + quickstart in Python/TS, 2) auth patterns we recommend, 3) sandbox env & CI secrets, 4) short demo of Console + Optimize hints. Any changes?
[00:00:28] Simon Green: Sounds good. Also want to touch on cost vs latency — our product is latency-sensitive.
[00:00:32] Jordan Lee: We'll call that out. Priya, take it away.

[00:00:36] Priya Nambiar: Ok opening my screen (repo link pasted in chat: https://redwood.ai/quickstart/northfield-sandbox) -- note that's a tracking link, real repo will be shared after the call. First file is the Python quickstart: requirements.txt, example env, and simple runner that calls the Redwood client for text generation.
[00:00:52] Priya Nambiar: The code snippet uses our python client: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_KEY')) -- simple, the SDK handles streaming, chunking, and retries out of the box.
[00:01:06] Carlos Mendes: Quick question, we use GCP secrets manager today. Can we integrate with KMS/Secret Manager?
[00:01:12] Priya Nambiar: Yes. For hosted API you'd store the REDWOOD_KEY in your secret manager and inject into CI. For Private/VPC deployments we support customer KMS integrations and HSM options as part of our enterprise package — you'll see integration notes under /docs/security.
[00:01:24] Asha Patel: Do you support Workload Identity for GKE?
[00:01:27] Priya Nambiar: We do; there's a short guide for GCP Workload Identity in the repo. Also service account to secret mapping is shown.

[00:01:33] Jordan Lee: I'll jump in briefly: for rotation, best practice is short-lived keys in CI and rotate via your secret manager, and we also support API key rotation via the Console with audit logs.
[00:01:43] Carlos Mendes: Audit logs are important for our compliance reviewers. Is there an exportable audit stream?
[00:01:47] Priya Nambiar: Yes, Console -> Organization -> Audit logs; you can stream to BigQuery or S3. For Private we can enable longer retention and centralize logs to your SIEM.

[00:01:56] Priya Nambiar: Back to the repo: TypeScript example uses the same patterns, env var REDWOOD_KEY, and we show two instantiation options — simple client and advanced client with retry/batching config.
[00:02:08] Asha Patel: What about local dev? We prefer not to commit keys and want a local sandbox token.
[00:02:12] Priya Nambiar: Repo includes a dev-token flow. You can create a short-lived sandbox token via Console that is scoped to a sandbox project; that's what we usually recommend for onboarding devs.

[00:02:22] [02:30] Priya Nambiar: (walks through code) Here's the part where we demonstrate streaming in Python; you call client.generate_stream(...) and we show client-side callback to update UI. Note: streaming chunk sizes may vary with the model and tokenization.
[00:02:39] Carlos Mendes: Any gotchas with tokenization across languages? We have mixed English + French content.
[00:02:44] Priya Nambiar: Mostly it's about encoding — use UTF-8; models handle multilingual but you should test for degenerate cases. We'll include a short eval set for you to run.

[00:02:52] [05:00] Priya Nambiar: Now auth deep-dive: three modes we recommend — 1) API keys (fastest for hosted), 2) SSO/SAML for Console access and team management, 3) Private deployment with VPC + customer KMS for sensitive data.
[00:03:10] Simon Green: For SSO, do you support SCIM for user provisioning?
[00:03:14] Priya Nambiar: Yes, SAML and SCIM; we can turn on Just-In-Time provisioning too.
[00:03:18] Asha Patel: Security team will ask about encryption in transit + at rest.
[00:03:22] Priya Nambiar: TLS everywhere; at rest we use AES-256, keys managed by Redwood in hosted mode, or customer-managed KMS for Private. We'll attach our security pack (SOC2 report + architecture diagram).

[00:03:29] [07:10] Jordan Lee: quick interjection — on billing & cost attribution: the Console lets you slice cost by token, by model, and by route. That helps map to product features. Also Optimize will suggest batching and cache TTLs to reduce per-token cost.
[00:03:43] Carlos Mendes: Can Optimize be run against our test traffic? We want to make sure we won't regress quality.
[00:03:48] Priya Nambiar: Yes, Optimize supports running on a copy of your traffic; it will surface suggested quantization, batching sizes, and model variants along with a quality delta. We keep evals tied to prompt sets so you can gate rollouts.

[00:03:56] [09:00] Priya Nambiar: Demo time—I'm switching to Console. (screen) Here's the quickstart sandbox project, keys panel, and how to create an API key scoped to generation only. I'll create a dev key now (redacted token in chat). This key is set to expire in 24 hours.
[00:09:20] Asha Patel: Nice. How about rate limits for that key?
[00:09:23] Priya Nambiar: You can set per-key rate limits, and apply route policies or per-team quotas. For dedicated customers you also get reserved throughput.

[00:09:30] [12:06] Priya Nambiar: Back to SDK: CI example shows GitHub Actions workflow that pulls REDWOOD_KEY from GitHub secrets, runs smoke tests against the sandbox endpoint, and tears down. We also show a policy to fail builds if latency increases above a threshold.
[00:09:50] Carlos Mendes: We use GitLab. Do you have examples for GitLab CI?
[00:09:54] Priya Nambiar: Yes the repo has both GitHub and GitLab snippets. The important bit is short-lived tokens and never writing secrets to logs.

[00:09:59] [15:00] Priya Nambiar: Now a short section on Private/VPC: customers who need network isolation use Private — we deploy a control plane that's customer-managed and optionally an on-prem package. There's a setup checklist: network CIDR, peering, firewall rules, and KMS details. For low-latency regional compliance we can pin to a region.
[00:15:18] Simon Green: Latency numbers—what should we expect for a 1k token generation on a dedicated box versus hosted?
[00:15:23] Priya Nambiar: It's model dependent; for a 1k token span on a high-throughput model, dedicated with pinned GPUs can be ~300–500 ms per 100 tokens in optimistic cases, but again depends on model, quantization and kernel choices. For hosted, we provide p95 SLAs for certain tiers — we can share the benchmark matrix.
[00:15:40] Jordan Lee: We'll include our latency/cost curves and the specific model variants we recommend for conversation vs long-form generation.

[00:15:48] [18:05] Priya Nambiar: Quick Optimize tips: prefer small batching for latency-critical routes, enable prefix KV caching for repeated completions, and use quantized model variants if you can tolerate small accuracy drops. The console shows expected savings per config change.
[00:16:05] Carlos Mendes: Do you have quantized 4-bit variants available publicly?
[00:16:09] Priya Nambiar: We partner with several open models and host quantized variants. Optimize will simulate quality deltas for each quant profile.

[00:16:20] [22:00] Priya Nambiar: Walkthrough of quickstart tests: run pytest or npm test against the sample prompts. We also have a run-evals script that computes rouge/bleu and a simple embedding similarity check for retrieval use cases.
[00:16:35] Asha Patel: That eval script—can it run in CI against a golden baseline?
[00:16:38] Priya Nambiar: Yes that's our recommended pattern: baseline on a known good commit and fail CI on regressions. We hook into the Console to flag rollouts.

[00:16:46] [26:30] Carlos Mendes: Let's talk about canary/A-B rollouts. We want to route 10% to a new quantized model first.
[00:16:53] Priya Nambiar: Absolutely, our routing policies let you do traffic splits by percentage, region, and even request attributes. There's also automatic fallback to a more expensive model if latency spikes or errors increase.
[00:17:01] Simon Green: Do we need dedicated instances for canaries?
[00:17:04] Priya Nambiar: Not necessarily, you can run canaries on compatible hosted capacity; however for strict SLOs dedicated is recommended.

[00:17:10] [32:00] Priya Nambiar: Security review points we heard so far: audit log export, long retention for Private, SCIM/SAML, KMS integration, and traffic egress controls. We'll attach our security whitepaper and SOC2 report.
[00:17:25] Jordan Lee: I'll coordinate with our security team to get the checklist responses.

[00:17:33] [36:15] Carlos Mendes: Ok, two practical items: 1) share the quickstart repo and a branch with our sample prompts, 2) run a small hosted vs dedicated benchmark on our sample prompt set (we can provide a 1000-query set).
[00:17:44] Jordan Lee: Noted. Priya, can you own the benchmark?
[00:17:47] Priya Nambiar: Yes I can run a baseline and return latency/cost per request; I'll include recommended batching and quant profiles.

[00:17:53] [40:00] Asha Patel: Another infra question—what network egress patterns exist? If we host in our VPC, where does traffic originate?
[00:40:07] Priya Nambiar: For Private we deploy into your VPC or on-prem and traffic stays inside the network. For Hosted, calls go to our regional endpoints; you can set IP allowlists and private peering for hybrid setups.

[00:40:18] [45:48] Priya Nambiar: Quick demo of the SDK error handling: we return structured error codes and rate-limit headers. The SDK has exponential backoff and jitter; we show how to hook into events to log prom metrics.
[00:40:34] Carlos Mendes: Can we integrate traces with our existing APM?
[00:40:37] Priya Nambiar: Yes we provide tracing hooks (OpenTelemetry) so you can tie Redwood spans into your existing traces.

[00:40:46] [48:00] Jordan Lee: We're almost at time — recap and next steps: I will send the quickstart repo + security pack by Monday (2025-12-01). Priya will run the benchmark and give recommendations by Friday (2025-12-05). Carlos will share the 1k prompt set by Wednesday (2025-12-03). We will schedule a pilot kickoff the week of 2025-12-08.
[00:48:59] Simon Green: That timeline works for us.

[00:49:05] [50:12] Priya Nambiar: Quick note — there are small transcription artifacts in the demo, e.g., some proper nouns in the Console can be slightly misrecognized, we'll include clear links in the follow-up email.
[00:49:18] Asha Patel: Great thanks everyone.
[00:49:22] Jordan Lee: Thanks team, we'll follow up with the materials.
[00:49:26] Carlos Mendes: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
